parliamentary affair

PDFs

and can't be reliably extracted into structured form — the question asked, the government's answer and reasoning, the decision, the people involved. Documents vary hugely: born-digital, scanned, some with handwritten stamps/signatures, tables and annexes. Generic document AI (e.g. Docling) gives a clean but domain-agnostic page representation; ad-hoc LLM prompting produces a different JSON shape for every body. b

middle layer

and

title: Extraction gap.
b
Turning heterogeneous, multilingual, partly-scanned PDFs into that format at 300,000-document scale needs an LLM — and an unconstrained, untraceable LLM invents values.

title: The main criterion is
insight
b

: does the team reach a well-founded conclusion on whether a common schema for parliamentary affairs is feasible, which parts can be represented consistently across parliaments, and where fundamental differences remain? A convincing negative or partial answer counts as success. If a workable schema emerges, demonstrate it on a broad, diverse set of real documents — showing an LLM can reliably transform heterogeneous PDFs into the schema across document types, languages and levels of government.

sLce: No restriction. For reference, the production stack is Python (FastAPI, Pydantic) with PostgreSQL and an Angular/React front end; ETL pipelines use Apache Hop.

Develop locally to start. OpenParlData runs on a self-managed VPS with a GitLab deploy process; ~20 GB RAM available for self-hosted LLMs on prod, though a specific LLM provider (e.g. Infomaniak) is intended. A dedicated container can later be added to OpenParlData's docker-compose landscape.
